# Getting started {#sec-start}

biyos is a C library with a C++ core. It builds with CMake, links into a program through one C header, and comes with a Python package that calls the same library. This chapter builds it, links a first program and runs it from Python.

## Building {#sec-start-build}

biyos needs CMake 3.25 or later and a compiler for C99 and C++20. Continuous integration builds it with GCC on Ubuntu 24.04, Clang on macOS 15 and MSVC on Windows Server 2022. From a clone of the repository:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --parallel
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure
```

The configure step downloads GoogleTest for the tests. Three options change the build:

| Option | Default | Effect |
| ------------------------ | -------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `BUILD_SHARED_LIBS` | `ON` | build `biyos` as a shared library; `OFF` builds a static one |
| `BIYOS_BUILD_TESTS` | `ON` | build the tests and register them with CTest |
| `BIYOS_WARNINGS_AS_ERRORS` | `OFF` | treat every compiler warning as an error |

The library lands in `build/lib`, as `libbiyos.so` on Linux and `libbiyos.dylib` on macOS. On Windows `biyos.dll` lands in `build/bin` and its import library in `build/lib`, each in a folder named for the configuration when the generator is Visual Studio. The header stays in `include/biyos`.

The install step copies the library, the header and a CMake package into a prefix:

```sh
cmake --install build --prefix "$PWD/install"
```

The examples in `examples` are a project of their own, built and tested against such a prefix:

```sh
cmake -S examples -B build/examples -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$PWD/install"
cmake --build build/examples
ctest --test-dir build/examples --output-on-failure
```

## The library and its header {#sec-start-layers}

A program sees one header, `biyos/biyos.h`, which includes only `<stddef.h>` and `<stdint.h>`. The shared library exports the functions of that header and nothing else: the C++ code behind them is compiled into the library with hidden symbols, so no C++ type or exception ever reaches the caller. The Python package loads the same library and calls the same functions.

![The layers of biyos. Each arrow points from a part to one it uses. Only `biyos.h` crosses the library's boundary.](../figures/layers.svg){#fig-layers}

Inside, each module may use only the modules below it, as @fig-layers shows. The repository's `tools/layers.txt` holds this order as data, and a check run by continuous integration refuses any include that breaks it.

## A first program {#sec-start-program}

This program prints the version of the library, then creates an environment and frees it:

```{.c file="examples/c/start.c"}
```

An environment holds the options, the event stream and the last error of each thread, and every model is made on one. Every call that acts returns a status, `BIYOS_OK` on success, and [Errors](#sec-errors) explains the others.

### With CMake

A CMake project finds an installed biyos as a package. The package accepts only the exact version it was built as:

```cmake
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)
project(app LANGUAGES C)

find_package(biyos 0.1.0 EXACT CONFIG REQUIRED)

add_executable(app app.c)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE biyos::biyos)
```

Configured with `-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$PWD/install`, the project builds against that copy.

The target `biyos::biyos` carries the include directory, so `#include <biyos/biyos.h>` works as written. Built as a static library, with `BUILD_SHARED_LIBS` set to `OFF`, it also carries the definition `BIYOS_STATIC`, which a program on Windows needs so that it does not look for the functions in a DLL.

### Without CMake

On Linux, a program compiles against the header and links the library from the build tree:

```sh
cc -std=c99 start.c -I biyos/include -L biyos/build/lib -lbiyos \
   -Wl,-rpath,"$PWD/biyos/build/lib" -o start
./start
```

which prints `biyos 0.1.0`.

## From Python {#sec-start-python}

The Python package lives in `interfaces/python`. It builds against an installed biyos of the same version, found as a CMake package, and places a copy of its library inside the package. That install is the shared library of a Release build, as [Building](#sec-start-build) makes it:

```sh
CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$PWD/install" python -m pip install ./interfaces/python
```

It needs Python 3.10 or later and no other package at run time. Each call goes through `ctypes` to the C API, so Python and C share every rule of this book. The first program becomes

```{.python file="interfaces/python/examples/start.py"}
```

The `with` block frees the environment when it ends. [The Python package](#sec-python) covers the package.
